summary: An early working paper on how hosts on the ARPANET might account for and administer network use, such as who is charged for what. It does not take a position; it identifies the issues for further discussion, considering current practices and new technical possibilities.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 136 is an early working paper about accounting for network use and host services. It sets out assumptions and questions for discussion, but does not recommend a specific accounting policy.

sections.title: Why Accounting Needs Discussion
sections.content:
Robert Kahn says a plan for host accounting in the ARPA Network must be formulated and agreed upon. The plan should consider existing host accounting practices as well as new technical contributions.

The RFC is an early attempt to identify issues for discussion and explicitly says it is not a position on them.
sections.plainLanguage: The network needs a plan for accounting, but this note does not choose one. It collects questions so the community can discuss what the plan should cover.

sections.title: Assumptions About Hosts and the Subnet
sections.content:
The paper assumes some entity will operate the subnet as a cost center and that hosts or ARPA will reimburse its costs. It describes the network as a government-sponsored resource-sharing network rather than a common carrier, and assumes both ARPA and non-ARPA-supported contractors may eventually connect.

It assumes each serving host will arrange payment for its facilities and provide information about usage costs. It also suggests postponing standard automated accounting until non-automated procedures are understood and stable, while allowing early experiments.
sections.plainLanguage: The author lists assumptions to frame the discussion, including who might operate the subnet and how hosts might arrange payment. These are assumptions in the paper, not decisions adopted by the network.

sections.title: Questions for the Network Community
sections.content:
The suggested topics include current host accounting practices, user access and security, the relationship between host and network accounting, long-term billing procedures, and whether some activities should be exempt from accounting.

The paper also asks whether accounting data should travel over the network or be available in real time, what technical mechanisms are needed for remote use, and whether conventional login is appropriate for every kind of activity. The list is explicitly not complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper asks who should pay, what usage to count and how access should be handled. It also asks whether accounting should happen online and invites additional topics.
